title: Hypertension: Measure Correctly, Confirm the Diagnosis, Treat Risk
bottomLine: Current Hypertension Canada primary-care guidance defines adult hypertension as blood pressure at or above 130/80 mm Hg when measured with a validated device under optimal standardized conditions. Confirm the diagnosis with out-of-office measurement when appropriate, then decide treatment from BP level, cardiovascular risk, comorbidity, tolerability and patient goals rather than one casual office reading.
recognize: Hypertension is commonly asymptomatic; symptoms such as focal neurologic deficit, pulmonary edema or acute chest/aortic syndromes suggest an emergency complication rather than 'symptomatic chronic hypertension'.
White-coat and masked hypertension make home or ambulatory measurements clinically important.
differentiate: Chronic hypertension is different from hypertensive emergency, which requires acute target-organ injury.
Abrupt, resistant or unusually early hypertension plus hypokalemia, renal clues, episodic adrenergic symptoms, sleep-apnea clues or drug/substance exposure raises secondary-cause suspicion.
assessment: Repeat BP using correct cuff size, standardized positioning/rest and a validated automated device; assess orthostasis when clinically relevant.
Review NSAIDs, stimulants, decongestants, estrogen-containing therapy, corticosteroids, alcohol, licorice and other contributors.
Assess ASCVD, diabetes, CKD, smoking, sleep apnea, family history, diet/activity and treatment-access barriers.
workup: Use out-of-office BP to confirm hypertension or detect white-coat/masked patterns when feasible.
Perform routine cardiovascular-risk/end-organ assessment and reserve secondary-cause testing for a compatible history/laboratory phenotype.
management: Recommend healthy lifestyle changes for all adults with hypertension.
Hypertension Canada recommends pharmacotherapy at BP ≥140/90 mm Hg and at systolic BP 130–139 mm Hg when cardiovascular risk is high.
For treated hypertension, target systolic BP below 130 mm Hg when well tolerated under the current primary-care guideline; individualize for orthostasis, frailty, pregnancy and competing illness.
medicationSafety: ACE inhibitors and ARBs are contraindicated in pregnancy and require renal function/potassium monitoring after initiation or clinically meaningful titration.
Avoid routine ACE-inhibitor plus ARB combination therapy.
Do not intensify treatment from one nonstandardized reading when home/ambulatory data and symptoms suggest overtreatment.
counselling: Teach validated home-BP technique and ask patients to record readings rather than checking repeatedly when anxious.
Discuss sodium, activity, alcohol, smoking and weight without stigma.
followUp: After initiation/titration, reassess BP, adverse effects and indicated labs promptly enough to achieve control safely.
examTrap: Diagnosing chronic hypertension from one rushed office reading or treating severe asymptomatic BP as an IV-drug emergency without looking for acute organ injury.
oneLinePearl: Measure correctly, confirm outside the office, then treat BP in the context of cardiovascular risk.

title: Heart Failure Across EF: Confirm the Syndrome, Then Treat the Phenotype
bottomLine: Heart failure is a clinical syndrome supported by structural/functional cardiac evidence; EF classifies the phenotype but does not establish or exclude HF by itself. HFrEF uses foundational disease-modifying therapy, whereas heart failure with non-reduced EF uses current phenotype/comorbidity-directed therapy plus congestion management.
recognize: Orthopnea, PND, edema, elevated JVP, pulmonary congestion and rapid weight gain support congestion; cool extremities, hypotension, confusion and oliguria suggest low-output physiology.
Preserved/non-reduced EF does not exclude HF when filling pressures, structural disease and the clinical syndrome support it.
differentiate: BNP/NT-proBNP support probability but are affected by age, AF, renal disease and obesity.
Peripheral edema alone is nonspecific; venous disease, renal/hepatic disease and medications can mimic congestion.
assessment: Assess volume status, perfusion, BP, rhythm, oxygenation, medication use/adherence, ischemia and common decompensation triggers.
Review NSAIDs, dietary sodium/fluid issues, arrhythmia, infection, renal injury and uncontrolled hypertension.
workup: Use ECG, renal/electrolyte/CBC and cause-directed testing plus echocardiography to define EF/structure.
Assess ischemia, iron deficiency, thyroid disease and other reversible contributors when indicated.
management: For HFrEF, introduce the four foundational disease-modifying classes as tolerated: ARNI/ACEi/ARB, evidence-based beta blocker, MRA and SGLT2 inhibitor; use diuretics for congestion.
For symptomatic HF with LVEF >40%, use the current 2025 CCS/CHFS HFnrEF framework and address congestion plus cardiorenal/comorbidity drivers.
Escalate acute pulmonary edema, shock, significant renal injury or refractory congestion to hospital-level care.
medicationSafety: Monitor BP, renal function and potassium during RAAS/ARNI/MRA/diuretic therapy.
Do not initiate/aggressively titrate beta blockade during cardiogenic shock or severe unstable decompensation.
SGLT2 inhibitors require sick-day/perioperative counselling and euglycemic-DKA awareness.
counselling: Teach symptom/weight monitoring, NSAID avoidance and medication purpose; clarify when worsening breathlessness/edema requires urgent assessment.
followUp: Use planned medication/lab titration and reassess EF/device eligibility when indicated after optimized therapy.
examTrap: Calling a normal EF 'no heart failure' or using diuresis alone in HFrEF without disease-modifying therapy.
oneLinePearl: Heart failure is a syndrome; EF selects the treatment framework, not whether HF exists.

title: Atrial Fibrillation: Stabilize, Prevent Stroke, Then Choose Rate or Rhythm Strategy
bottomLine: AF management has three simultaneous questions: is the patient unstable, does stroke prevention require anticoagulation, and is rate control or rhythm control the better symptom/outcome strategy? Confirm AF electrocardiographically and do not let a successful cardioversion erase anticoagulation-risk assessment.
recognize: AF is an irregular atrial rhythm confirmed on ECG/rhythm recording and can present with palpitations, dyspnea, fatigue, chest discomfort, HF or embolic events.
AF may be intermittent; a normal office ECG does not exclude paroxysmal AF when symptoms/risk justify monitoring.
differentiate: Hemodynamic instability attributable to AF requires urgent synchronized cardioversion.
Atrial flutter, multifocal atrial tachycardia, frequent ectopy and sinus arrhythmia are not interchangeable with AF.
assessment: Assess hemodynamics, symptoms, duration/onset certainty, HF/valve disease, thyroid/alcohol/OSA triggers, prior stroke/TIA and bleeding risk.
Use the current Canadian stroke-prevention framework (including CHADS-65-based guidance where applicable) rather than assuming age alone or sinus restoration ends risk.
workup: Use ECG and ambulatory monitoring when intermittent; obtain electrolytes/renal/thyroid and echocardiography according to the clinical context.
Before elective cardioversion, address AF duration and thromboembolic protection using the current pathway.
management: Choose rate control when it adequately controls symptoms/physiology and rhythm control when symptoms, HF/tachycardia-mediated dysfunction, early strategy or other patient factors support it.
Use anticoagulation when indicated by Canadian stroke-risk guidance, with agent choice determined by valve disease, renal function, pregnancy, interactions and bleeding risk.
Refer complex rhythm-control/ablation decisions to cardiology/electrophysiology.
medicationSafety: Avoid AV-nodal blockers that worsen pre-excited AF or advanced conduction disease.
DOACs are not interchangeable with warfarin in mechanical valves or selected significant rheumatic mitral stenosis contexts.
Antiarrhythmics have structural-heart, QT, renal and interaction constraints.
redFlags: Ischemia or acute HF from AF
Very rapid ventricular response with instability
counselling: Explain that rhythm control treats rhythm/symptoms but stroke prevention is a separate decision.
Address alcohol, sleep apnea, BP, weight and activity risk factors without framing AF as patient-caused.
followUp: Reassess rate/rhythm burden, anticoagulant safety/adherence, renal function and symptom response; ensure cardioversion/ablation follow-up is closed-loop.
examTrap: Stopping anticoagulation simply because sinus rhythm was restored or choosing rate/rhythm therapy before assessing instability and stroke risk.
oneLinePearl: AF care is stability + stroke prevention + rhythm strategy—three decisions, not one.

title: Acute Coronary Syndrome: ECG and Serial Troponin Are Time-Critical
bottomLine: Suspected ACS requires rapid ECG, serial high-sensitivity troponin and immediate assessment for STEMI, instability and lethal alternative diagnoses. One normal early ECG or troponin does not safely exclude evolving ACS when the clinical syndrome remains concerning.
recognize: Pressure/heaviness, dyspnea, diaphoresis, nausea, unexplained fatigue or epigastric discomfort can be ischemic presentations.
Older adults, women and people with diabetes may have less classic central chest pain.
differentiate: Aortic dissection, PE, tension pneumothorax, pericarditis/tamponade and esophageal rupture remain important dangerous alternatives.
Troponin-positive myocardial injury from sepsis, PE, myocarditis or tachyarrhythmia is not automatically plaque-rupture MI.
assessment: Assess ABCs/hemodynamics, onset/timing, ECG symptoms, bleeding risk, anticoagulant/antiplatelet use, cocaine/stimulants and features of aortic/PE alternative diagnoses.
Look for HF, shock and malignant arrhythmia.
workup: Obtain a 12-lead ECG promptly and repeat with symptom evolution; use the local validated serial high-sensitivity troponin algorithm.
Order imaging/other tests based on alternative diagnosis and complication risk without delaying reperfusion.
management: Activate the regional reperfusion pathway for STEMI and urgent acute-care/cardiology evaluation for high-risk NSTE-ACS.
Use guideline-directed antiplatelet/anticoagulant/anti-ischemic therapy after considering contraindications and competing diagnoses.
Transition survivors into secondary prevention and cardiac rehabilitation.
medicationSafety: Nitrates can worsen hypotension and are unsafe with recent PDE-5 inhibitor exposure or selected preload-dependent states.
Avoid reflex oxygen in a normoxemic patient; use oxygen for hypoxemia/respiratory distress.
Do not give fibrinolysis when aortic dissection is suspected.
counselling: Explain why symptoms that improve still require evaluation because ischemia can fluctuate before infarction.
followUp: Ensure post-ACS medications, rehabilitation, EF assessment and risk-factor follow-up are owned and completed.
examTrap: Sending home a concerning chest-pain patient because the first ECG or troponin is normal.
oneLinePearl: ACS is a serial diagnosis—ECG, troponin and clinical evolution all matter.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society ACS and Secondary Prevention resources

title: DVT and PE: Diagnose by Probability, Anticoagulate Safely, Decide Duration From Cause
bottomLine: VTE management starts with pretest probability and objective diagnosis, then anticoagulant selection, disposition and treatment duration based on DVT/PE severity, provoking factors, bleeding risk and persistent recurrence risks. Do not let a D-dimer or clot size replace clinical probability and physiology.
recognize: Unilateral leg swelling/pain and proximal tenderness can indicate DVT; acute dyspnea, pleuritic pain, syncope or unexplained hypoxemia/tachycardia can indicate PE.
Cancer, recent surgery/immobility, estrogen/pregnancy, prior VTE and inherited/acquired thrombophilia context alter probability and recurrence risk.
differentiate: D-dimer is useful primarily when pretest probability is low/intermediate enough that a negative test can rule out disease.
Superficial thrombophlebitis and chronic post-thrombotic symptoms are different from acute proximal DVT.
assessment: Assess hemodynamic stability, bleeding risk, renal/hepatic function, pregnancy, cancer, weight extremes, interacting drugs and prior VTE.
For PE, determine whether shock/RV strain or social/medical factors make outpatient treatment unsafe.
workup: Use compression ultrasound for DVT and CTPA or an appropriate alternative for PE according to probability/context.
Use D-dimer selectively rather than in clearly high-probability disease.
Thrombophilia testing is not routine after every VTE and should be ordered only when it can change management.
management: Treat confirmed DVT/PE with an appropriate anticoagulant; Thrombosis Canada notes DOACs are generally preferred over LMWH-to-warfarin strategies for many nonpregnant patients when not contraindicated.
Treat PE for at least the acute minimum duration, then individualize extended therapy based on provoked/unprovoked/persistent risk and bleeding risk.
High-risk PE with shock requires immediate reperfusion/specialist consideration.
medicationSafety: Anticoagulant choice depends on pregnancy, renal function, cancer context, antiphospholipid syndrome, mechanical valves, interactions and bleeding risk.
Do not use INR to monitor DOAC effect or assume normal PT/aPTT excludes clinically relevant exposure.
counselling: Teach adherence, bleeding precautions, recurrence symptoms and when interruptions for procedures require a specific plan.
followUp: Document provoking factors and duration decision; reassess bleeding/recurrence risk and persistent dyspnea/post-thrombotic symptoms.
examTrap: Ordering D-dimer for a high-probability swollen leg or stopping anticoagulation simply because the first three months are complete without reviewing whether the VTE was provoked or persistent-risk.
oneLinePearl: VTE has three decisions: probability/diagnosis, safe anticoagulation, and duration based on why the clot happened.
sourceBasis: Thrombosis Canada Pulmonary Embolism Treatment Guide — version May 2025

title: Dyslipidemia: Select Statin Intensity From Vascular Risk and Treatment Context
bottomLine: Lipid therapy is cardiovascular-risk therapy. Established ASCVD and other statin-indicated/high-risk conditions drive treatment more than the isolated LDL value; use maximally tolerated statin therapy where indicated, assess response/adherence, and add evidence-based nonstatin therapy when residual risk and guideline thresholds justify it.
recognize: Established ASCVD is secondary prevention and generally warrants intensive LDL-lowering unless contraindicated or inconsistent with goals of care.
Diabetes, CKD, markedly high LDL/familial hypercholesterolemia and calculated risk can create primary-prevention treatment indications.
differentiate: Primary prevention is not the same treatment context as post-MI/PAD/stroke secondary prevention.
Very high triglycerides create pancreatitis risk and require a different immediate priority than LDL-focused prevention.
assessment: Assess ASCVD, diabetes, CKD, smoking, BP, family history, prior statin response, pregnancy potential, interacting drugs and secondary dyslipidemia causes.
Clarify muscle symptoms rather than immediately labeling permanent statin intolerance.
workup: Use a lipid profile and Canadian risk estimation when applicable; investigate secondary causes and familial dyslipidemia when the pattern is severe/unexpected.
CK and liver tests are ordered when clinically indicated rather than as indiscriminate serial monitoring for every stable patient.
management: Use appropriate statin intensity for secondary/high-risk prevention and reassess LDL response/adherence after initiation/intensification.
Add ezetimibe/other evidence-based therapy when guideline thresholds and residual risk warrant it after maximally tolerated statin therapy.
Address smoking, BP, diabetes and activity/nutrition simultaneously.
medicationSafety: Review clinically important CYP/transporter interactions and assess severe muscle weakness/dark urine promptly.
Pregnancy/planning pregnancy requires medication-specific lipid-therapy review rather than automatic continuation.
counselling: Explain absolute vascular benefit and that medication selection is about preventing events rather than treating one laboratory result.
followUp: Repeat lipids after clinically meaningful treatment changes and periodically once stable; address adherence, cost and adverse effects.
examTrap: Withholding indicated statin therapy because LDL looks only mildly elevated in a patient with established vascular disease—or ordering routine CK at every visit in an asymptomatic patient.
oneLinePearl: Choose lipid therapy from the patient's vascular risk, then use the lipid panel to confirm response.

title: Syncope: Risk-Stratify the Collapse Before Calling It Vasovagal
bottomLine: Syncope is transient loss of consciousness from global cerebral hypoperfusion. The priority is identifying cardiac, hemorrhagic, thromboembolic and other dangerous causes before diagnosing benign vasovagal or orthostatic syncope; ECG and event history are core, while routine neuroimaging is low value without neurologic/trauma indications.
recognize: Vasovagal syncope often has a trigger/prodrome and rapid recovery; orthostatic syncope follows postural BP/volume/medication physiology.
Exertional syncope, abnormal ECG, structural heart disease or family history of sudden death raises cardiac risk.
differentiate: Seizure often has prolonged postictal confusion or stereotyped features; hypoglycemia/intoxication can mimic transient LOC.
Brief convulsive movements can occur during syncope and do not automatically diagnose epilepsy.
assessment: Obtain patient/witness event history, posture/trigger/prodrome, recovery, injury, chest symptoms, bleeding, medications and family history.
Perform cardiovascular/neurologic examination and orthostatic vitals when safe/appropriate.
workup: Obtain ECG for all clinically significant syncope and use glucose/CBC/electrolytes or pregnancy testing when indicated.
Use telemetry/ambulatory monitoring/echo based on arrhythmic/structural suspicion.
Do not order routine CT head/EEG for uncomplicated syncope with normal neurologic assessment and no relevant trauma.
management: Hospital/emergency evaluation is appropriate for unstable patients, concerning ECG/structural disease, exertional syncope, major bleeding or other high-risk features.
Treat orthostatic/vasovagal contributors through medication/volume/trigger strategies when dangerous causes are reasonably excluded.
medicationSafety: Diuretics, nitrates, alpha blockers, antihypertensives and QT-/rate-affecting drugs can contribute and require medication reconciliation.
Do not suppress a compensatory tachycardia before excluding hemorrhage/sepsis/PE.
counselling: Discuss driving/work restrictions based on cause/risk and current Canadian/provincial rules; teach hydration/trigger strategies only after serious causes are addressed.
followUp: Ensure rhythm-monitor/echo/specialty results are closed-loop and revisit diagnosis if episodes recur.
examTrap: Ordering a CT head automatically for uncomplicated syncope or calling exertional syncope vasovagal without cardiac evaluation.
oneLinePearl: Syncope workup is risk stratification: history + ECG first, selective tests second.

title: Pericarditis and Myocarditis: Inflammation Can Mimic ACS and Destabilize Quickly
bottomLine: Pericarditis and myocarditis are clinical syndromes that can mimic ACS. Pericarditis is suggested by pleuritic/positional pain and compatible ECG/inflammation, whereas myocarditis can present with troponin elevation, arrhythmia or ventricular dysfunction; tamponade, malignant arrhythmia or HF makes either an urgent hospital-level problem.
recognize: Pericarditis pain is often pleuritic and improves sitting forward; diffuse ST/PR changes may occur but are not always present.
Myocarditis may follow viral/systemic illness and present with chest pain, dyspnea, arrhythmia, syncope or new HF.
differentiate: Regional ischemic ECG changes and coronary-pattern symptoms favor ACS, which still must be excluded when clinically plausible.
Troponin elevation occurs in myocarditis but does not by itself distinguish inflammatory from ischemic injury.
Pericardial effusion is not synonymous with tamponade; tamponade is hemodynamic compromise.
assessment: Assess hemodynamics, JVP, pulsus/heart sounds, HF, rhythm/syncope, recent infection/vaccination/drug/autoimmune history and exertional symptoms.
Look for instability before focusing on etiology.
workup: Use ECG, troponin, inflammatory markers and echocardiography; use cardiac MRI/specialist testing for suspected myocarditis or diagnostic uncertainty when appropriate.
Investigate ischemia/PE/other causes when presentation overlaps.
management: Treat uncomplicated pericarditis with evidence-based anti-inflammatory therapy when appropriate and activity restriction/follow-up.
Suspected myocarditis with HF, arrhythmia or significant biomarker/imaging abnormality needs cardiology assessment and exercise restriction.
Tamponade or hemodynamic compromise requires emergency drainage/specialist care.
medicationSafety: NSAID/colchicine use requires renal/GI/pregnancy/interaction review.
Avoid strenuous exercise during active myocarditis/pericarditis until recovery/return guidance is satisfied.
Do not treat myocarditis troponin elevation as routine ACS antithrombotic therapy without evaluating the actual diagnosis.
redFlags: Persistent severe chest pain with diagnostic uncertainty
counselling: Teach recurrence/return symptoms and the need for temporary exercise restriction when myocarditis/pericarditis is active.
followUp: Reassess symptoms, inflammatory/cardiac findings and ventricular function; specialist clearance guides return to strenuous activity after myocarditis.
examTrap: Calling every troponin-positive chest pain NSTEMI or assuming a pericardial effusion equals tamponade without hemodynamic compromise.
oneLinePearl: Pericarditis is inflammation around the heart; myocarditis is injury in the heart—both can mimic ACS, and physiology determines urgency.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society cardiovascular-inflammatory/imaging practice resources
